By viewing multivariate intensity functions as infinite-dimensional matrices or tensors within function spaces, our algorithms attain the optimal bias-variance trade-off, yielding rate-optimal estimation error, with model complexity governed by matrix or tensor ranks. They substantially improve estimation accuracy, while simultaneously reducing computational cost. To illustrate the adaptivity of the proposed framework, we show that many fundamental classes of multivariate functions, including additive and mean-field models, admit finite-rank tensor representations. We apply our method to a four-dimensional U.S. Geological Survey earthquake dataset, comprising features such as latitude, longitude, depth, and magnitude. Our tensor estimator recovers localized seismicity patterns (California, Oklahoma, Pacific Northwest, north-central U.S.), whereas the kernel baseline oversmooths them.

papers.title: Bivariate Copula Models With Event-Free Cure Effect for Survival Extrapolations and Individual-Level Correlation Analysis
papers.authors: Daniel J Sharpe, Georgia Yates, Tuli De, Renuka Kandikatla, Prianka Singh, Matthew Dixon, Kiran Davé, Jackie Vanderpuye-Orgle, Murat Kurt
papers.abstract: OBJECTIVES: Overall survival (OS) extrapolations from mixture cure models (MCMs) are often sensitive to the cure fraction, which is challenging to estimate when data are immature. Furthermore, in some cancer populations, it may be unreasonable to assume curative effects among patients who are not event-free. We addressed these problems using bivariate copula MCMs to jointly model OS and progression- (PFS) or recurrence-free survival (RFS), with a single event-free cure fraction parameter. METHODS: We proposed a practical framework for parametric survival copula model selection and interpretation, which involves estimating five representative candidate copula functions and examining OS distributions conditioned on intermediate event times. Bivariate MCMs with event-free cure fraction, based on previously selected marginal distributions, were estimated for two studies of nivolumab with contrasting survival patterns, namely, in previously treated advanced esophageal squamous cell carcinoma (OS-PFS correlation) and resected melanoma (OS-RFS correlation). RESULTS: OS extrapolations from bivariate MCMs with an effective PFS (or RFS) cure fraction were more conservative than from univariate MCMs. Although patient-level OS-PFS/RFS correlation coefficients were sensitive to the copula, model averaging and inspecting estimated conditional OS distributions enabled clinically meaningful inference on the prognostic impact of intermediate events. CONCLUSIONS: Bivariate MCMs with event-free cured subpopulation incorporated curative effects into OS extrapolations more cautiously than conventional MCMs, based on a more rapidly maturing composite endpoint. The model is especially useful when OS data are immature and if post-event cure is clinically implausible. Employing alternative copulas that cover archetypal association patterns mitigated model selection bias in patient-level correlation analysis.

papers.title: Two-Stage Estimation for Causal Inference Involving Semi-Continuous Exposures
papers.authors: Xiaoya Wang, Richard J Cook, Yeying Zhu, Tugba Akkaya-Hocagil, R Colin Carter, Sandra W Jacobson, Joseph L Jacobson, Louise M Ryan
papers.abstract: Methods for causal inference are well developed for binary and continuous exposures, but in many settings, the exposure has a substantial mass at zero-such exposures are called semi-continuous. We propose a general causal framework for such semi-continuous exposures, together with a two-stage estimation strategy. A two-part propensity structure is introduced for the semi-continuous exposure, with one component for exposure status (exposed vs unexposed) and another for the exposure level among those exposed, and incorporates both into a marginal structural model that disentangles the effects of exposure status and dose. The two-stage procedure sequentially targets the causal dose-response among exposed individuals and the causal effect of exposure status at a reference dose, allowing flexibility in the choice of propensity score methods in the second stage. We establish consistency and asymptotic normality for the resulting estimators, and characterize their limiting values under misspecification of the propensity score models. Simulation studies evaluate finite sample performance and robustness, and an application to a study of prenatal alcohol exposure and child cognition demonstrates how the proposed methods can be used to address a range of scientific questions about both exposure status and exposure intensity.

papers.title: Online Updating Mixture Cure Models for Large-Scale Survival Data Streams
papers.authors: Li Jin, Tao Hu, Liming Xiang
papers.abstract: The growing availability of large-scale survival data streams present significant challenges for statistical inference particularly in the presence of a cure fraction, which complicates estimation and increases computational burden. To address these challenges, we propose an online updating mixture cure model framework. Our approach employs a batchwise renewable estimation procedure that aggregates historical information into summary statistics to update the model without retaining historical individual-level data, and thus eliminating the need for full data storage. A renewable penalized expectation-maximization algorithm is developed to enable simultaneous parameter estimation and variable selection. Furthermore, a tuning-free strategy is incorporated to enhance computational efficiency. The asymptotic properties of the proposed method are established. Simulation studies and an application to breast cancer data from the Surveillance, Epidemiology, and End Results database demonstrate the method's estimation accuracy, predictive performance, and computational scalability.

papers.title: Developing an Innovative Jackknife Estimator for Quantifying Between-Study Variance in Meta-Analysis of Proportions
papers.authors: Muhammad Mohsin, Stephan Morgenthaler
papers.abstract: The DerSimonian and Laird (DL) method, commonly used in meta-analysis, often underestimates the between-study variance. The underestimation causes the confidence intervals to have less than the expected 95% coverage, resulting in inconclusive research findings. The present study introduces the use of the jackknife technique to improve the DL between-study variance estimator for meta-analyses of proportions from single-arm studies, as well as suggests certain transformations in combination with the jackknife technique. The proposed methodology is intended for settings in which the parameter of interest is an event probability or proportion, particularly for small numbers of studies with large variation. Simulation studies for binomial observations are conducted to compare the relative biases and coverage probabilities of the mean ( μ ) obtained by the DL, Paule and Mandel (PM), Restricted Maximum Likelihood (REML), and Hartung-Knapp-Sidik-Jonkman (HKSJ) methods with our proposed DerSimonian and Laird jackknife (DLJ) and transformed DerSimonian and Laird jackknife (TDLJs) methods. The simulation results show that our proposed DLJ and TDLJ estimators better quantify the between-study variance in meta-analysis of binary events, especially for small numbers of studies with larger variation and high probability of μ respectively. Three real life examples are presented to determine the performance of our new proposed between-study variance estimators.

papers.title: Can discrete-time analyses be trusted for stepped wedge trials with continuous recruitment?
papers.authors: Hao Wang, Guangyu Tong, Heather Allore, Kelsey L Grantham, Monica Taljaard, Fan Li
papers.abstract: In stepped wedge cluster randomized trials (SW-CRTs), the intervention is rolled out to clusters sequentially over multiple periods. It is common practice to analyze data from SW-CRTs using linear mixed models that treat time as discrete. However, a recent systematic review found that 95.1% of cross-sectional SW-CRTs recruit individuals continuously over time. Despite the prevalence of continuous recruitment, there has been limited guidance on how to draw model-robust inference for such designs. In this article, we conduct simulation studies to examine the performance of discrete-time linear mixed models in the case of continuous recruitment designs with a continuous outcome. Specifically, we generate outcomes under a continuous-time exponential decay correlation structure with either discrete or continuous fixed period effects. We consider constant and exposure-time-dependent intervention effects, with and without random intervention effects across clusters. We then analyze the simulated data using linear mixed models under three discrete-time working correlation structures: simple exchangeable, nested exchangeable, and discrete-time exponential decay, with robust sandwich variance estimation. Our results demonstrate that discrete-time analysis often yields negligible bias and that the robust variance estimator with the Mancl and DeRouen correction consistently achieves nominal coverage and type I error rate. However, when recruitment patterns vary systematically between control and intervention periods, discrete-time analyses give slightly biased intervention effect estimates. Finally, we illustrate these findings by reanalyzing a completed SW-CRT.

papers.title: Using fractional derivatives to derive marginal densities
papers.authors: S Y Li, D A van Dyk, M Autenrieth
papers.abstract: This paper presents a novel method for analytical derivations of marginal densities using the fractional derivatives of moment-generating functions. Although the method requires likelihood functions to take specific forms, its assumptions are otherwise modest. It only requires that the prior moment-generating functions exist, are finite, and are continuous and differentiable at certain points. We also present the probabilistic and statistical insights behind this method.

papers.title: Test of partial effects for Fréchet regression on Bures-Wasserstein manifolds
papers.authors: Haoshu Xu, Hongzhe Li
papers.abstract: We propose a novel test for assessing partial effects in Fréchet regression on the Bures-Wasserstein manifold. Under the null hypothesis, we show that the statistic admits a degenerate V-statistic approximation whose limiting distribution is aweighted mixture of chi-squared random variables, with weights determined by the eigenvalues of an integral operator associated with a reproducing kernel Hilbert space (RKHS) kernel. We establish the asymptotic validity and consistency of the proposed test. Its finite-sample performance is examined through simulation studies.We apply the proposed test to study the effect of age, while controlling for other covariates, on gene co-expression structure in single-cell data.

papers.title: Sensitivity Analysis for the Test-Negative Design
papers.authors: Soumyabrata Kundu, Peng Ding, Jingshu Wang, Xinran Li
papers.abstract: The test-negative design has become popular for evaluating the effectiveness of post-licensure vaccines using observational data. In addition to its logistical convenience on data collection, the design is also believed to control for the differential health-care-seeking behavior between vaccinated and unvaccinated individuals, an important while often unmeasured confounder between the vaccination and infection. Hence, the design has been employed routinely to monitor seasonal flu vaccines and more recently to measure the COVID-19 vaccine effectiveness. Despite its popularity, the design has been questioned, in particular about its ability to fully control for the unmeasured confounding. In this paper, we explore deviations from a perfect test-negative design, and propose various sensitivity analysis methods for estimating the effect of vaccination measured by the causal odds ratio on the subpopulation of individuals with good health-care-seeking behavior. We start with point identification of the causal odds ratio under a test-negative design, comparing different forms of identification assumptions and their corresponding estimands. We then propose two approaches for conducting sensitivity analysis, addressing the influence of the unmeasured confounding in two different ways. Specifically, one approach investigates partial control for unmeasured confounding in the test-negative design, while the other examines the impact of unmeasured confounding on both vaccination and infection. Furthermore, we combine these approaches to provide narrower bounds on the true causal odds ratio, and further sharpen the bounds by restricting the treatment effect heterogeneity. Finally, we apply the proposed methods to evaluate the effectiveness of COVID-19 vaccines using observational data from test-negative designs.

papers.title: POLAR: A Pessimistic Model-based Policy Learning Algorithm for Dynamic Treatment Regimes
papers.authors: Ruijia Zhang, Xiangyu Zhang, Zhengling Qi, Yue Wu, Yanxun Xu
papers.abstract: Dynamic treatment regimes (DTRs) provide a principled framework for optimizing sequential decision-making in domains where decisions must adapt over time in response to individual trajectories, such as healthcare, education, and digital interventions. However, existing statistical methods often rely on strong positivity assumptions and lack robustness under partial data coverage, while offline reinforcement learning approaches typically focus on average training performance, lack statistical guarantees, and require solving complex optimization problems. To address these challenges, we propose POLAR, a novel pessimistic model-based policy learning algorithm for offline DTR optimization. POLAR estimates the transition dynamics from offline data and quantifies uncertainty for each history-action pair. A pessimistic penalty is then incorporated into the reward function to discourage actions with high uncertainty. Unlike many existing methods that focus on average training performance or provide guarantees only for an oracle policy, POLAR directly targets the suboptimality of the final learned policy and offers theoretical guarantees, without relying on computationally intensive minimax or constrained optimization procedures. To the best of our knowledge, POLAR is the first model-based DTR method to provide both statistical and computational guarantees, including finite-sample bounds on policy suboptimality. Empirical results on both synthetic data and the MIMIC-III dataset demonstrate that POLAR outperforms state-of-the-art methods and yields near-optimal, history-aware treatment strategies. *(abstract via OpenAlex)*

papers.title: Localizing support-set changepoints in high-dimensional linear models
papers.authors: Junfeng Cui, Junhui Wang, Changliang Zou, Yan Zhou
papers.abstract: Existing changepoint localization methods for high-dimensional regression models typically focus on scenarios where the regression coefficients follow a piecewise constant structure over time. However, this assumption can be overly restrictive in many practical applications due to the complex temporal dynamics of the coefficients. Additionally, in sparse regression models, the primary interest sometimes lies not in changes in the magnitudes of the coefficients, but rather in identifying the time points at which covariates transition between inactive and active states. In this paper, we propose a simple yet effective method for detecting changepoints in the support set, allowing the coefficients to vary continuously over time. Theoretically, we establish the minimax lower bound on the localization error that nearly matches the upper bound achieved by the proposed method, and show that the required signal-to-noise condition is essentially the weakest possible based on the impossibility region in a minimax sense. Extensive numerical studies further demonstrate the superior performance of the proposed method. It is also applied in the analysis of real air quality data from Northern Taiwan in 2015. An R package "SCP" is developed to implement the proposed method.

papers.title: General Frameworks for Conditional Two-Sample Testing
papers.authors: Seongchan Lee, Suman Cha, Ilmun Kim
papers.abstract: We study the problem of conditional two-sample testing, which aims to determine whether two populations have the same distribution after accounting for confounding factors. This problem commonly arises in various applications, such as domain adaptation and algorithmic fairness, where comparing two groups is essential while controlling for confounding variables. We begin by establishing a hardness result for conditional two-sample testing, demonstrating that no valid test can have significant power against any single alternative without proper assumptions. We then introduce two general frameworks that implicitly or explicitly target specific classes of distributions for their validity and power. Our first framework allows us to convert any conditional independence test into a conditional two-sample test in a black-box manner, while preserving the asymptotic properties of the original conditional independence test. The second framework transforms the problem into comparing marginal distributions with estimated density ratios, which enables direct application of existing methods for marginal two-sample testing. We demonstrate this idea in a concrete manner with classification and kernel-based methods. Finally, simulation studies are conducted to illustrate the proposed frameworks in finite-sample scenarios.

papers.title: Bayesian multiple imputation for functional data
papers.authors: Ziren Jiang, Lei Xuan, Eric F Lock, Erjia Cui
papers.abstract: Missing data are pervasive in modern functional datasets, where trajectories are often sparsely or irregularly observed. Although functional principal component analysis is widely used to reconstruct incomplete curves, existing approaches typically employ single imputation, leading to overly optimistic inferences in downstream analyses. To address these challenges, we develop a novel Bayesian multiple imputation framework for functional data (BAMIFun). For single-level functional data, we impose a Bayesian low-rank model that incorporates penalized spline representations to enforce smoothness of the functional domain and derive an efficient Gibbs sampler algorithm for posterior computation. In addition, we demonstrate and validate how to properly account for estimation uncertainties in downstream analysis. Furthermore, we extend the framework to multiway functional data using Functional Tensor Singular Value Decomposition model, enabling Bayesian multiple imputation in settings not supported by existing methods. Simulation studies show that BAMIFun achieves substantially improved coverage and more reliable downstream inference compared to existing methods, while maintaining similar imputation accuracy. Case studies using a physical activity dataset and an infant gut microbiome dataset further demonstrate the practical advantages of our proposed methods under severe missingness.

papers.title: Asymptotic theory of the quadratic assignment procedure for dyadic data analysis
papers.authors: Lei Shi, Peng Ding
papers.abstract: The quadratic assignment procedure (QAP) is a popular tool for analysing dyadic data in medical and social sciences. To test the association between 2 dyadic measurements represented by 2 symmetric matrices, QAP calculates the p-value by permuting the units, or equivalently, by permuting the rows and columns of 1 matrix in the same way. Its extension to the regression setting, known as the multiple regression QAP, has also gained popularity, especially in psychometrics. However, the statistical theory for QAP has not been fully established in the literature. We fill the gap in this paper. We formulate the dyadic models underlying various QAPs. We derive (a) the asymptotic sampling distributions of some canonical test statistics and (b) the corresponding asymptotic permutation distributions induced by QAP under strong and weak null hypotheses. Task (a) relies on applying the theory of U-statistics, and task (b) relies on applying the theory of double-indexed permutation statistics. Our asymptotic theory combines tasks (a) and (b), and suggests that we must use properly studentized statistics in QAP to ensure that it is finite-sample exact under the strong null hypothesis and preserves the asymptotic type I error rate under the weak null hypothesis.

papers.title: A Tail Likelihood Ratio Method for Large-scale Causal Mediation Tests in Epigenome-Wide Studies
papers.authors: Haoyu Yang, Ruoyu Wang, Yuzhou Lin, Xihong Lin
papers.abstract: Large-scale mediation testing has attracted considerable attention in epigenome-wide studies, intending to determine whether the effect of an exposure on an outcome is mediated through specific DNA methylation sites. Statistical inference for the mediation effects is challenged by the complexity of testing a large number of composite null hypotheses. We propose a tail likelihood ratio (TLR) test that is robust to variations in the proportion of null cases, signal strength, and signal distribution, achieving higher power for marginal mediation testing than existing methods while maintaining robust error rate control across diverse scenarios, with false discovery rate control established theoretically under independence and supported by simulation under dependence. The proposed TLR method features a powerful test statistic whose distribution under the composite null is derived analytically. Meanwhile, since methylations are often correlated, we account for the correlation of dependent test statistics using a principal component-based approximation. Simulations demonstrate that the proposed method maintains accurate error rate control in multiple comparisons and exhibits power gains compared to existing methods. We apply the proposed method to the Normative Aging Epigenetic Study and identify 27 of the 484,548 CpG sites of DNA methylation measured on 632 men that mediate the effect of smoking on lung function. *(abstract via OpenAlex)*

papers.title: Uniform ergodicity and spectral gap of importance-tempered MCMC with heavy-tailed targets
papers.authors: Quan Zhou
papers.abstract: We study the importance-tempered random-walk Metropolis (RWM) algorithm on Rd, which targets the tempered density πβ(x)∝(π(x))β with β∈(0,1), and corrects for the resulting bias by importance weighting. The dynamics of this sampler can be described by a continuous-time Markov chain whose embedded chain is the tempered random-walk Metropolis. We prove that when the tails of π decay at rate ‖x‖−γ, this continuous-time chain is uniformly ergodic if and only if dγ<β<(γ−2)γ. Furthermore, the global spectral gap of this chain can be controlled via the spectral gap of the chain restricted to a ball with radius growing polynomially in d. Our theory and and simulation studies show that, with a suitable choice of β, importance tempering can substantially reduce sensitivity to initialization and significantly improve efficiency over the standard random-walk Metropolis.

papers.title: Enhancing visual interpretability and explainability in functional survival trees and forests
papers.authors: Giuseppe Loffredo, Elvira Romano, Fabrizio Maturo
papers.abstract: Functional survival models are key tools for analyzing time-to-event data with complex predictors, such as functional or high-dimensional inputs. Despite their predictive strength, these models often lack interpretability, which limits their value in practical decision-making and risk analysis. This study investigates two key survival models: the functional survival tree (FST) and the functional random survival forests (FRSFs). It introduces novel methods and tools to enhance the interpretability of FST models and improve the explainability of FRSF ensembles. Applications to simulated data and to a real intensive care dataset illustrate that the proposed approaches provide post-hoc graphical and functional summaries that facilitate the interpretation of FSTs and the explanation of forest-level predictions.

papers.title: Calibrated Bayes Analysis of Cluster-Randomized Trials
papers.authors: Ruyi Liu, Joshua L Warren, Yuki Ohnishi, Donna Spiegelman, Liangyuan Hu, Fan Li
papers.abstract: In cluster-randomized trials (CRTs), entire clusters of individuals are randomized to treatment, and outcomes within a cluster are typically correlated. While frequentist approaches are standard practice for CRT analysis, Bayesian methods have emerged as a strong alternative. Previous work has investigated the use of Bayesian hierarchical models for continuous, binary, and count outcomes in CRTs, but these approaches focus on model-based treatment effect coefficients as the target estimands, which may have ambiguous interpretation under model misspecification and informative cluster size. In this article, we introduce a calibrated Bayesian procedure for estimand-aligned analysis of CRTs even in the presence of potentially misspecified models. We propose estimators targeting both the cluster-average treatment effect (cluster-ATE) and individual-average treatment effect (individual-ATE), particularly in scenarios with informative cluster sizes. We additionally explore strategies for summarizing the posterior samples that can achieve the frequentist coverage even under working model misspecification. We provide simulation evidence to demonstrate the model-robustness property of the proposed estimators in CRTs, and further investigate the impact of covariate adjustment as well as the use of more flexible Bayesian nonparametric working models in the CRT context.

papers.title: Beyond vintage rotation: bias-free sparse representation learning with oracle inference
papers.authors: Chengyu Cui, Yunxiao Chen, Jing Ouyang, Gongjun Xu
papers.abstract: Learning low-dimensional latent representations is a central topic in statistics and machine learning, and rotation methods have long been used to obtain sparse and interpretable representations. Despite nearly a century of widespread use across many fields, rigorous guarantees for valid inference for the learned representation remain lacking. In this paper, we identify a surprisingly prevalent phenomenon that suggests a reason for this gap: for a broad class of vintage rotations, the resulting estimators exhibit a non-estimable bias. Because this bias is independent of the data, it fundamentally precludes the development of valid inferential procedures, including the construction of confidence intervals and hypothesis testing. To address this challenge, we propose a novel bias-free rotation method within a general representation learning framework based on latent variables. We establish an oracle inference property for the learned sparse representations: the estimators achieve the same asymptotic variance as in the ideal setting where the latent variables are observed. To bridge the gap between theory and computation, we develop an efficient computational framework and prove that its output estimators retain the same oracle property. Our results provide a rigorous inference procedure for the rotated estimators, yielding statistically valid and interpretable representation learning.

papers.title: A seamless dose-optimization design for monotherapy and combination therapy
papers.authors: Kentaro Takeda, Masahiro Kojima
papers.abstract: The emergence of molecular-targeted agents and immune-oncology therapies has fundamentally transformed oncology drug development, necessitating evolution beyond traditional dose-finding approaches designed for cytotoxic agents. While conventional agents exhibit predictable monotonic dose-response relationships, novel anticancer agents often demonstrate plateau-effect patterns where higher doses may compromise therapeutic benefit, requiring identification of optimal biological doses that balance efficacy and tolerability. The FDA's Project Optimus initiative emphasizes comprehensive dose optimization through parallel randomized cohorts and patient backfilling to better understand pharmacological profiles across multiple dose levels. Contemporary drug development increasingly prioritizes combination therapy alongside monotherapy evaluation, yet existing designs typically assume equivalent roles for both agents, diverging from clinical practice where novel agents combine with established treatments having limited dose options. This article proposes a seamless dose-optimization design that adaptively evaluates both monotherapy and combination therapy based on efficacy and toxicity outcomes through adaptive subtrials with patient backfilling capabilities. The model-assisted framework employs predetermined Bayesian optimal boundaries, eliminating real-time model fitting while accommodating evaluation of both monotherapy and combination therapy and enabling sequential enrollment with strategic backfilling. Simulation studies demonstrate robust performance across diverse dose-response patterns relevant to contemporary oncology. The design addresses critical gaps between methodological assumptions and clinical reality, offering a practical approach that integrates monotherapy and combination therapy evaluation with efficacy-toxicity-based backfilling. This framework ensures straightforward implementation while maintaining flexibility for complex dose-response relationships characteristic of novel anticancer agents, providing significant advantages for clinical implementation in the era of targeted and immune-oncology therapeutics.

papers.title: Blockwise dynamic selection of smoothing parameters for kernel estimators of nonstationary densities of streaming data
papers.authors: F Camirand Lemyre, A Delaigle, J Mao
papers.abstract: We consider nonparametric estimation of the nonstationary density of streaming data collected continuously over time. Those types of data are often available only for a limited time after being observed, for example due to storage or data privacy constraints. Therefore, analyzing them requires dynamic approaches that do not require repeated access to past data. A suitable iterative kernel estimator of nonstationary densities has been developed by Rutkowski (1989); it requires choosing important tuning parameters each time a new observation arises, for which no adequate practical selection criterion has been developed yet.We propose a data-driven dynamic selection of those parameters, which can be implemented iteratively and requires only sequential access to consecutive blocks of the most recent data. To choose the sizes of the blocks, we propose a theoretically founded approach based on properties of cross-validation criteria. We illustrate the broader potential of our ideas by suggesting a dynamic blockwise practical implementation of another kernel estimator of nonstationary densities developed by Hall et al. (2006).We apply our technique to simulated data and to light curve data from the NASA Kepler mission.

papers.title: A Factor Model Based Time-Varying Auto-Align Overlapping Clustering
papers.authors: Yanxin Jin, Peiyao Cai, Janice Chen, Yang Ning, Kean Ming Tan
papers.abstract: In many scientific fields such as genomics and neuroscience, data often exhibit complex structures where features can belong to multiple clusters simultaneously and vary over time. Traditional clustering methods such as k-means and hierarchical clustering typically assume static cluster structures and perform hard assignments, limiting their ability to capture the underlying overlapping and time-varying cluster structures. To address these challenges, we propose a novel time-varying Auto-Align clustering (AAclust) framework that effectively estimates and tracks dynamic changes in overlapping cluster memberships over time. Specifically, we employ a time-varying factor model, in which the overlapping cluster structures are modeled through a factor loading matrix that is allowed to vary over time. Theoretically, we show that the population factor loading matrix is identifiable up to a signed permutation across time, i.e., the population overlapping cluster memberships are identifiable. Furthermore, we show that our framework can consistently estimate the number of clusters and the overlapping cluster memberships for the features. By leveraging cross-covariance matrices between any two time points, our proposed method automatically aligns cluster labels over time without requiring post-hoc label matching based on similarity measures like the Rand index. We evaluate the performance of our proposed method through numerical experiments and an application to a functional magnetic resonance imaging dataset under continuous natural stimuli. *(abstract via OpenAlex)*

papers.title: Which Small-Sample Correction Should be Used When Analyzing Stepped-Wedge Designs With Time-Varying Treatment Effects?
papers.authors: Yongdong Ouyang, Monica Taljaard, James P Hughes, Fan Li
papers.abstract: Stepped‐wedge cluster randomized trials (SW‐CRTs) evaluate interventions that are sequentially rolled out across clusters. Standard analyses of SW‐CRTs typically use immediate‐treatment (IT) models, which assume the treatment effects begin at crossover and remain constant thereafter. When treatment effects vary with exposure duration, IT models may misrepresent the target effects. Exposure‐time indicator (ETI) models address this by allowing treatment effects to differ by time since exposure and can properly target the time‐averaged treatment effect (TATE) and long‐term effect (LTE). Like IT models, ETI models require specification of a random‐effects structure, which may be misspecified. While robust variance estimators (RVEs) theoretically protect against such misspecification, their empirical performance under ETI models is not well understood. We review RVEs for ETI models and evaluate them in comprehensive simulation studies with continuous and binary outcomes under correctly specified (binary only) and misspecified random‐effects structures. We compare the classic sandwich variance, Kauermann–Carroll (KC), Mancl–DeRouen (MD), and Morel–Bokossa–Neerchal (MBN) bias‐corrected sandwich variance estimators for inference on the TATE and LTE in primary simulations and additionally evaluate Fay–Graubard (FG) in a sub‐study. Our simulations show that under misspecified random‐effects structures, model‐based standard errors (SE) produced undercoverage, whereas RVEs improved performance under the ETI models. For continuous outcomes, MD with a t ‐distribution and degrees of freedom equal to the number of clusters minus two gave the closest to nominal coverage probabilities. Surprisingly, however, MBN was the only consistently reliable option for binary outcomes. MD, however, could be unstable in one‐cluster‐per‐sequence designs because of data sparsity. Across scenarios, both model‐based SE and RVE for LTE were unstable, indicating that greater caution is needed when targeting LTE under ETI models.

papers.title: Testing matrix factor structure via generalized likelihood ratio
papers.authors: Xinbing Kong, Liwen Zhang, Tong Zhang
papers.abstract: In this paper, we introduce a generalized likelihood ratio test for assessing whether the factor loading matrix in high-dimensional data exhibits a Kronecker structure, thereby offering a rigorous tool for validating two-way matrix factor models. A central challenge in likelihood-based inference for factor models arises from inherent rotational non-identifiability, which prevents the likelihood function from admitting a standard second-order Taylor expansion. To address this issue, we augment the quasi-likelihood with a quadratic identification penalty that removes rotational degeneracy locally. Building on this construction, we derive the asymptotic distribution of the proposed statistic under the null hypothesis and unveil a new Wilks-type phenomenon in a high-dimensional setting. Under the alternative hypothesis, we further establish the consistency of the test, demonstrating its ability to detect deviations from the Kronecker structure. Simulation studies demonstrate the finite-sample effectiveness of the proposed method. Furthermore, applications to real datasets illustrate the practical utility of the proposed procedure by assessing the presence of Kronecker structure in factor loading matrices.

papers.title: Semiparametric learning from open-set label shift data
papers.authors: Siyan Liu, Yukun Liu, Qinglong Tian, Pengfei Li, Jing Qin
papers.abstract: We study the open-set label shift problem, where the test data may include a novel class absent from the training data. This setting is challenging because both the class proportions and the distribution of the novel class are not identifiable without extra assumptions. Existing approaches often rely on restrictive separability conditions, prior knowledge, or computationally infeasible procedures, and some may lack theoretical guarantees. We propose a semiparametric density ratio model framework that ensures identifiability while allowing overlap between novel and known classes. Within this framework, we develop maximum empirical likelihood estimators and confidence intervals for class proportions, establish their asymptotic validity, and design a stable Expectation–Maximization algorithm for computation. We also develop a goodness-of-fit test for model assessment and an approximately optimal classifier with theoretical guarantees. Simulations and a real-data application confirm that our methods improve both estimation accuracy and classification performance compared with existing approaches.

papers.title: Partially Linear Additive Reversed Mean Model for Panel Count Data With Informative Terminal Event
papers.authors: Anyin Feng, Xiangbin Hu, Wen Su, Xingqiu Zhao
papers.abstract: This article investigates a partially linear additive reversed mean model for panel count data with an informative terminal event. By anchoring the time origin at the terminal event, the proposed model characterizes the recurrent event process prior to the occurrence of the terminal event. The partially linear additive form provides a flexible framework for modeling covariate effects. The B-spline sieve approximation is employed for both the baseline reversed mean function and the link function. To make the optimization of the loss function feasible, we treat the distribution function of the terminal event as a nuisance functional parameter and develop a two-stage estimation procedure. We establish the asymptotic properties of the proposed estimator, including consistency, convergence rate, and asymptotic distribution. Simulation studies demonstrate that the proposed estimator performs well in finite-sample settings. The proposed method is further illustrated through an application to the Chinese longitudinal healthy longevity survey (CLHLS).

papers.title: Marginal Analysis of Clustered Interval-Censored Competing Risks Data With Informative Cluster Size
papers.authors: Xinyi Wang, Peijie Wang, Xinyuan Song
papers.abstract: Motivated by the National Alzheimer's Coordinating Center (NACC) study, this paper addresses the marginal analysis of clustered data under a complex setting involving interval censoring, competing risks, and informative cluster size, for which existing methods are not readily applicable. We consider a class of marginal generalized odds-rate transformation models for the cumulative incidence function in the presence of interval-censored competing risks, with the Fine-Gray model and the sub-distribution proportional odds model included as special cases. For statistical inference, a cluster-weighted sieve maximum pseudo-likelihood estimation procedure is developed, in which B-splines are used to approximate the nonparametric components of the semiparametric models. This method effectively reduces the original infinite-dimensional estimation problem to a finite-dimensional one. We establish the asymptotic properties of the resulting parameter estimators and conduct extensive simulation studies to evaluate their finite-sample performance. The proposed methodology is applied to the motivating NACC data to investigate potential risk factors for the cumulative incidence of Lewy body dementia.

papers.title: Bayesian Methods Incorporating Baseline Covariates for Borrowing Historical Control Data in Randomized Clinical Trials: A Neutral Comparison Study
papers.authors: David Jesse, Diane Uschner, Markus C Elze, Tim Friede, Francois Mercier
papers.abstract: The idea of leveraging historical control data in randomized clinical trials (RCTs) has gained a lot of attention, in particular for rare disease and pediatric indications where conducting traditional and fully powered RCTs can be challenging. In this regard, Bayesian dynamic borrowing (BDB) methods, which adapt the amount of borrowing based on the outcome heterogeneity between the current and historical data, are well established. In recent years, an increasing number of related methods have been published that combine the BDB framework with approaches that account for baseline covariates. The underlying rationale is that some of the heterogeneity may be explained systematically by variations in the distributions of these characteristics. While many such methods are now available, direct comparisons of them are scarce and there is no consensus on which one can be considered the state of the art. We address this issue by conducting a neutral comparison of three methods of this class, namely the propensity score weighted commensurate prior, propensity score weighted multi-source exchangeability models, and Bayesian additive regression trees. We assess their performance for continuous outcomes through extensive simulations and further evaluate them using two examples based on real RCT data. Our study reveals potential issues with some of these approaches and provides recommendations for choosing a particular method for real RCTs.

papers.title: An Integrative Approach for Subtyping Mental Disorders Using Multimodal Data
papers.authors: Yinjun Zhao, Yuanjia Wang, Ying Liu
papers.abstract: Understanding the biological and behavioral heterogeneity underlying psychiatric disorders is critical for advancing precision diagnosis, treatment, and prevention. This paper addresses the scientific question of how multimodal data, which spans clinical, cognitive, and neuroimaging measures, can be integrated to identify biologically meaningful subtypes of mental disorders. We introduce Mixed INtegrative Data Subtyping (MINDS), a Bayesian hierarchical model designed to jointly analyze mixed-type data for simultaneous dimension reduction and clustering. Using data from the adolescent brain cognitive development (ABCD) Study, MINDS integrates clinical symptoms, cognitive performance, and brain structure measures to subtype attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) and obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD). Our method leverages Pólya-Gamma augmentation for computational efficiency and robust inference. Simulations demonstrate improved stability and accuracy compared to existing clustering approaches. Application to the ABCD data reveals clinically interpretable subtypes of ADHD and OCD with distinct cognitive and neurodevelopmental profiles. These findings show how integrative multimodal modeling can enhance the reproducibility and clinical relevance of psychiatric subtyping, funding data-driven policies for early identification and targeted interventions in mental health.

papers.title: Addressing Missing Data in Clinical Trials With a Hybrid Control Arm
papers.authors: Joshua Wasserman, Herbert Pang, Jiawen Zhu
papers.abstract: Randomized trials have long been the standard for evaluating experimental treatments in medical and pharmacological studies, but the associated time and cost have spurred research into designs that augment randomized studies with data from external sources. Hybrid control arms offer the promise of improved precision-at the possible expense of bias-by forming a control arm from patients randomized to control along with historical controls or patients found in a registry. Although recent reviews have published guidance on minimizing and addressing missing data in clinical trials, the issue has received little attention in the context of trials with a hybrid control arm. We propose novel treatment effect estimators that handle missing outcomes in both the trial and external control datasets, even when the missingness patterns differ between them. These estimators are built from augmented weighted estimating equations and are doubly robust when outcomes are missing at random (MAR). In addition, we introduce a sensitivity analysis using a pattern-mixture model to assess robustness of the effect estimates under violations of the MAR assumption. We compare these estimators to a popular parametric modeling technique through simulation and an application to a real-world trial.

papers.title: Joint modeling of longitudinal measurements and survival outcomes in heart valve transplantation data
papers.authors: Avinash Kumar, M S Panwar, Sushil Kumar
papers.abstract: A joint modeling technique for longitudinal data and time-to-event data is advanced statistical methodology to analyze repeated measurements and time-to-event outcomes. In the present article, a shared random effects approach is considered to account for both longitudinal data and survival outcomes. The longitudinal data is submodeled by a linear mixed-effects model that captures the individual response over time. Whereas the time-to-event sub-model uses the generalized exponential distribution as the baseline distribution for the proportional hazard model to incorporate survival times as well as time-independent covariates. To estimate model parameters, the Expectation-Maximization approach has been used, which is effective with latent random effects since random effects are unobservable in nature. In the E-step, the expected log-likelihood is derived based on current parameter estimates, and in the M-step, we maximize this likelihood to update the parameters. To show the efficacy of the proposed approach, an extensive simulation study has been conducted. Furthermore, the model is tested on a real-world medical dataset, heart valve data, to demonstrate its efficacy in analyzing the link between longitudinal responses and survival outcomes.

papers.title: Estimating Marginal Odds Ratios for Cluster Randomized Trials: The Cluster-Level GLM
papers.authors: Jennifer A Thompson, Brennan C Kahan, Andrew Copas
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: Methods for estimating marginal effects in cluster randomized trials are limited. We describe and evaluate a cluster-level generalized linear model (CL-GLM) that applies a GLM to cluster-level summaries (means, proportions, or rates) and can estimate differences, ratios, or odds ratios. We focus on odds ratios. METHODS: We conducted a simulation study with 10-50 clusters, intracluster correlation coefficients of 0.05 or 0.15, and a mean cluster size of 120, either fixed or variable. Informative cluster size, where the intervention effect varies with cluster size, was also considered. Control arm prevalence was set to 50%. We compared cluster-level GLMs with normal and gamma distributions and logit link to generalized estimating equations (GEE) and independence estimating equations (IEEs). Weighted and unweighted analyses were examined to target cluster-average and individual-average estimands. RESULTS: CL-GLM with a normal distribution produced unbiased marginal cluster-average odds ratios with appropriate confidence interval coverage. CL-GLM with a gamma distribution resulted in over-coverage. Unweighted IEE produced unbiased marginal individual-average odds ratios with correct coverage. GEE was unbiased when cluster size was uninformative but biased under informative cluster size. Weighted CL-GLM led to under-coverage, whereas weighted IEE resulted in over-coverage. The CL-GLM had similar power to GEE and unweighted IEE. CONCLUSIONS: The cluster-level GLM with a normal distribution provides a robust alternative to estimating equation approaches for marginal odds ratios in cluster randomized trials, with good performance under both informative and uninformative cluster size and no loss of power. We recommend the cluster-level GLM with a normal distribution when the marginal cluster-average estimand is of interest, and unweighted IEEs when the marginal individual-average estimand is of interest.

papers.title: A multivariate Bayesian biomarker screening algorithm that incorporates clinical covariates
papers.authors: Maria Veronica Vinattieri, Federico Panero, Qingchun Jin, Anna Sf Lok, Francesco C Stingo, Nabihah Tayob
papers.abstract: Advanced hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) has limited treatment options and poor survival. Early detection of HCC improves survival, but current ultrasound screening is inconsistent and poorly adhered to. Biomarker-based blood tests offer a more accurate, accessible, and reliable alternative. Recent developments in methods for early detection of HCC have focused on the trajectories of multiple biomarkers, assuming that biomarkers follow a joint hierarchical mixture model with random changepoints. We extend this model, allowing covariates to influence three aspects of the model: biomarker trajectories, diagnosis times, and subject-specific prior risks. We evaluated whether covariates could capture unexplained heterogeneity in biomarker levels to improve early detection. A Markov chain Monte Carlo algorithm was implemented to derive posterior distributions used in risk calculations among future patients and to determine whether a patient has a positive screen. The screening algorithm was evaluated through simulation studies under a range of possible covariate extensions. The Hepatitis C Antiviral Long-term Treatment against Cirrhosis (HALT-C) trial was used to further study the proposed biomarker screening algorithms for HCC using cross-validation.

papers.title: Variable Selection for Additive Global Fréchet Regression
papers.authors: Haoyi Yang, Satarupa Bhattacharjee, Lingzhou Xue, Bing Li
papers.abstract: We present a novel framework for variable selection in Fréchet regression with responses in general metric spaces, a setting increasingly relevant for analyzing non-Euclidean data such as probability distributions and covariance matrices. Building on the concept of (weak) Fréchet conditional means, we develop an additive regression model that represents the metric-based discrepancy of the response as a sum of covariate-specific nonlinear functions in reproducing kernel Hilbert spaces (RKHS). To address the absence of linear structure in the response space, we transform the response via squared distances, enabling an interpretable and tractable additive decomposition. Variable selection is performed using Elastic Net regularization, extended to the RKHS setting, and further refined through a local linear approximation scheme that incorporates folded concave penalty functions. We establish theoretical guarantees, including variable selection consistency and the strong oracle property, under minimal assumptions tailored to metric-space-valued responses. Simulations and applications to distributional and matrix-valued data demonstrate the scalability, interpretability, and practical effectiveness of the proposed approach. This work provides a principled foundation for statistical learning with random object data. *(abstract via OpenAlex)*

papers.title: Semi-supervised Clustering Through Representation Learning of High-dimensional Count Data
papers.authors: Linshanshan Wang, Mengyan Li, Zongqi Xia, Molei Liu, Tianxi Cai
papers.abstract: High-dimensional count data arise in many modern applications, such as electronic health records (EHR) and RNA sequencing, with sparse, heterogeneous observations driven by complex latent structure. These characteristics make modeling and prediction challenging, especially when labels are limited. We propose SCORE, a semi-supervised representation learning framework for clustering and embedding construction from high-dimensional count features. SCORE is built on a Poisson-adapted latent factor mixture model that supports incorporating external pre-trained feature embeddings when available, enabling efficient extraction of latent cluster membership and low-dimensional representations. To scale inference and learning to large datasets, SCORE uses a hybrid algorithm that combines expectation-maximization with a Gaussian variational approximation, leveraging a small labeled subset to refine estimation on a large pool of unlabeled samples. We establish convergence guarantees for this hybrid procedure, quantify approximation errors introduced by the Gaussian variational approximation, and derive error rates under increasing embedding dimensions. Our theory and experiments show that incorporating unlabeled data improves accuracy and reduces sensitivity to label scarcity, yielding strong finite-sample performance relative to existing approaches. We demonstrate SCORE for predicting disability status in multiple sclerosis using EHR data, where it learns informative patient embeddings with strong predictive performance, highlighting its practical value. *(abstract via OpenAlex)*

papers.title: Modeling Amplitude and Phase Variation of Multivariate Random Processes in Metric Spaces*
papers.authors: Yaqing Chen, Kyum Kim
papers.abstract: In functional data analysis, distinguishing between amplitude and phase variation is essential to prevent distorted statistical inferences. While extensive work has been devoted to developing time-warping methods to address this issue for Euclidean functional data, much less is known about how to characterize and model these two sources of variability when they co-exist in random processes taking values in general metric spaces. In this paper, we develop a comprehensive statistical framework characterizing amplitude and phase variation for multivariate metric-space-valued functional data. We propose a geodesic latent deformation model (GLDM) for jointly analyzing both types of variation by using tools from metric geometry, and define tempo indices to quantify the temporal dynamics. We devise a novel estimation procedure and establish (uniform) convergence rates for the model estimators. The method’s broad applicability is demonstrated through a real-world application to annual gender-specific age-at-death distributions providing new insights into global longevity dynamics as well as simulations on multivariate positive semi-definite (PSD) matrix-valued and network-valued functional data. *(abstract via OpenAlex)*

papers.title: Confounder-robust causal discovery and inference in Perturb-seq using proxy and instrumental variables
papers.authors: Kwangmoon Park, Hongzhe Li
papers.abstract: Emerging single-cell technologies that combine CRISPR-based genetic perturbations with single-cell RNA sequencing, such as Perturb-seq, offer unprecedented opportunities to uncover cause-and-effect relationships among genes. Nonetheless, Perturb-seq experiments are subject to unobserved factors that, if not properly handled, can severely bias the inferred causal relationships between genes. These latent factors may arise not only from intrinsic molecular features of the regulatory elements, but also from unmeasured genes omitted due to cost-constrained experimental designs. Although methods for analyzing large-scale Perturb-seq data are rapidly maturing, approaches that explicitly account for such unobserved confounders when inferring causal gene networks are still lacking. Here, we propose a novel approach to accurately reconstruct causal gene networks from Perturb-seq data even when important confounders are missing. Our framework leverages proxy and instrumental variable strategies to exploit the rich information embedded in the perturbations, enabling unbiased estimation of the underlying directed acyclic graph (DAG) of gene expression. Applications to both comprehensive synthetic data and real CRISPR interference experiments in K562 cells demonstrate that our method outperforms baseline approaches that lack principled adjustments for unmeasured confounding, yielding more accurate and biologically relevant recovery of the true causal DAGs. *(abstract via OpenAlex)*

papers.title: Bayesian Statistical Methods: With Applications to Machine Learning, 2nd ed
papers.authors: Bruno Sansó
papers.abstract: Brian J. Reich and Sujit K. Ghosh. Boca Raton, FL: Chapman & Hall/CRC Press, 2026, xii + 347 pp., $140.99(H), ISBN: 978-1-032-48632-1.The second edition of Reich and Ghosh’s book is a compact and a... *(abstract via OpenAlex)*

papers.title: A Spatial Interference Approach to Account for Mobility in Air Pollution Studies with Multivariate Continuous Treatments
papers.authors: Heejun Shin, Danielle Braun, Kezia Irene, Michelle Audirac, Joseph Antonelli
papers.abstract: We develop new methodology to improve our understanding of the causal effects of multivariate air pollution exposures on public health accounting for mobility. Typically, in environmental health studies, exposure to air pollution for an individual is assigned based on their residential address, though many people spend time in different regions with potentially different levels of air pollution. To account for this, we incorporate estimates of the mobility of individuals from cell phone mobility data to obtain a more accurate estimate of their air pollution exposure. We treat this as an interference problem, where individuals in one geographic region can be affected by exposures in other regions due to mobility into those areas. We propose policy-relevant estimands and derive expressions showing the extent of bias one would obtain by ignoring individuals’ mobility. We additionally highlight the benefits of the proposed interference framework relative to a measurement error framework to account for mobility. Utilizing flexible Bayesian methodology we develop novel estimation strategies to estimate causal effects that account for this spatial spillover. Lastly, we use the proposed methodology to study the health effects of ambient air pollution on mortality among Medicare enrollees in the United States. *(abstract via OpenAlex)*

papers.title: A Generalized Tangent Approximation based Variational Inference Framework for Strongly Super-Gaussian Likelihoods
papers.authors: Somjit Roy, Pritam Dey, Debdeep Pati, Bani K. Mallick
papers.abstract: Variational inference, as an alternative to Markov chain Monte Carlo sampling, has played a transformative role in enabling scalable computation for complex Bayesian models. Nevertheless, existing approaches often depend on either rigid model-specific formulations or stochastic black-box optimization routines. Tangent approximation is a principled class of structured variational methods that exploits the geometry of the underlying probability model. However, its utility has largely been confined to logistic regression and related modeling regimes. In this article, we propose a novel variational framework based on tangent transformation for a broad class of probability models characterized by strongly super-Gaussian likelihoods. Our method leverages convex duality to construct tangent minorants of the log-likelihood, thereby inducing conjugacy with Gaussian priors over model parameters in an otherwise intractable setup. Under mild assumptions on the data-generating mechanism, we establish algorithmic convergence guarantees, a contribution that stands in contrast to the limited theoretical assurances typically available for black-box variational methods. Additionally, we derive near-parametric variational risk bounds. Superior performance of our proposed methodology is illustrated on simulated and real-data scenarios that challenge state-of-the-art variational algorithms in terms of scalability and their ability to consistently capture complex underlying data structure. *(abstract via OpenAlex)*

papers.title: Valid Inference for Two Sample Summary Statistics Mendelian Randomization
papers.authors: Kai Wang, Grace Z Wang
papers.abstract: Mendelian randomization (MR) studies increasingly rely on summary statistics from genome-wide association studies (GWASs). However, current summary-data methods treat marginal GWAS effect estimates as independent across instrumental single-nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs), which holds only when the SNPs have no effect. Without imposing this independence assumption, we derive expressions for the two-stage least squares (TSLS), two-sample TSLS (TSTSLS), and generalized method-of-moments estimators together with their variance estimators using only GWAS summary statistics, assuming the instrumental SNPs are in linkage equilibrium. We show that the widely used inverse-variance weighted (IVW) estimator is generally not equivalent to either TSLS or TSTSLS, contrary to a common claim in the MR literature. We further demonstrate that the conventional IVW standard error is generally inconsistent and provide a consistent alternative. Extensive simulations confirm the theoretical results and reveal that Wald confidence intervals based on summary statistics can be anti-conservative. An application to publicly available GWAS summary statistics on body mass index and systolic blood pressure illustrates the practical implications of the proposed methodology.

papers.title: Federated Time-to-Event Data Analysis Using Piecewise Exponential Regression in DataSHIELD
papers.authors: Bodil Svennblad, Benedicte Delcoigne, Paul Burton, Demetris Avraam
papers.abstract: Time-to-event analyses on individual patient data are commonly performed with Cox or Poisson regression. The statistical power of epidemiological findings from such analyses is often sufficient when a large amount of data is analyzed, especially when studying rare outcomes or rare exposures. The increase of sample size can be achieved by co-analyzing data collected from different cohorts and hosted at different locations. For co-analyzing data located at different centers, the common options are either (i) to physically transfer and pool the data into a single dataset and analyze them jointly or (ii) to conduct a two-step meta-analysis where a separate analysis is done at each center and the center-specific results are then pooled and combined into a single estimate. DataSHIELD offers a third option where individual patient data from different locations are analyzed in a federated manner without transporting any data. In this paper, we describe how a federated Poisson regression can be conducted on time-to-event data using this infrastructure, providing relevant estimates.

papers.title: Dynamic Prediction in Mixture Cure Models: A Model-Based Landmarking Approach
papers.authors: Marta Cipriani, Marco Alfò, Mirko Signorelli
papers.abstract: Mixture cure models are widely used in survival analysis when a portion of patients is considered cured and is no longer at risk for the event of interest. In clinical settings, dynamic survival prediction is particularly important to refine prognosis by incorporating patient information updated over time. Landmarking methods have emerged as a flexible approach for this purpose, as they allow to summarize longitudinal covariates up to a given landmark time and use these summaries in subsequent prediction. For mixture cure models, the only landmarking strategy available in the literature relies on summarizing the dynamics of observed longitudinal markers through the last observation carried forward (LOCF) method. However, LOCF discards most of the longitudinal information, does not correct for measurement error, and may rely on outdated values if observation times are far apart. To overcome these limitations, we propose a sequential approach that integrates model-based landmarking within a mixture cure model. Initially, longitudinal covariates are modeled using (generalized) linear mixed models, from which individual-specific summaries are predicted. The predicted summaries are then incorporated as covariates into a Cox proportional hazards cure model. We investigated the performance of the proposed approach under different cure fractions, sample sizes, and longitudinal data structures through an extensive simulation study. The results show that the model-based strategy provides more refined predictions compared to LOCF, even when the model is misspecified in favor of the LOCF approach. Finally, we illustrate our method using a real-world dataset on renal transplant patients.

papers.title: Calibrating Machine Learning Approaches for Probability Estimation Without Calibration Data
papers.authors: Eleonora Di Carluccio, Georgios Koliopanos, Francisco M Ojeda, Christian Weimar, Andreas Ziegler
papers.abstract: Statistical prediction models for binary outcomes are becoming increasingly popular. One significant challenge is calibrating these models to suit the characteristics of a target population that is structurally different from the original population. Calibration is especially challenging when there is no training data available from the target population. To address this problem, we propose a novel calibration method, SimCal, which uses synthetic data generated from the model development data in conjunction with marginal statistics from the calibration cohort. We show that expert judgment modeling (EJM) may be used for calibration if cross-sectional data from the target population are available comprising expert judgments about the potential outcome and the covariates. We describe three alternative calibration approaches when calibration data are lacking: similarity-binning averaging (SBA), adaptive calibration of predictions (ACP), and Elkan calibration. In a simulation study, we compare SBA, ACP, Elkan calibration, and SimCal. R code for applying these methods is provided from the re-analysis of data on coronary artery disease. We illustrate all 5 calibration approaches with a real data set for predicting functional outcome after stroke and all approaches but EJM in the re-analysis of the Cleveland Clinic data. None of the approaches performed convincingly well in all situations. SimCal performed well when model parameters were correctly specified. EJM failed on the stroke data. Further research is urgently required for calibration in the absence of calibration data.

papers.title: Locally Estimated Scatterplot Smoothing for Censored Survival Data
papers.authors: David van Klaveren, Peter C Austin, Patrick W Serruys, Ben van Calster, Frank E Harrell
papers.abstract: In the absence of censoring, locally estimated scatterplot smoothing (LOESS) is a powerful tool to estimate the relationship between a continuous covariate and the probability of an event and is often used to visually assess calibration of prognostic models. Since follow-up in prognostic studies is often incomplete, we aimed to study the extension of LOESS to right-censored data. In line with other work, we first obtained inverse-probability-of-censoring (IPC) weights through Kaplan-Meier estimation. When censoring varied by covariate levels, we used Cox regression with a spline function of the covariate to obtain IPC weights. We then applied LOESS to the weighted event indicators to estimate the relationship between the covariate and the probability of an event within a specific time horizon. We illustrated the application of LOESS for censored data (LOESScd) using patients with complex coronary artery disease. We used the LOESScd to estimate the association between continuous predictors and the probability of death within 10 years. LOESScd estimates closely followed grouped Kaplan-Meier estimates, especially in case of weak smoothing. Covariate-dependent IPC weights improved LOESScd when censoring varied by covariate levels. We then examined the finite-sample behavior of LOESScd in simulations motivated by four typical prognostic model validation scenarios. In 2000 samples of 1800 patients, bias was limited and coverage was close to nominal. In conclusion, LOESScd is a promising estimator of the relationship of a continuous covariate with the probability of an event in the presence of right-censoring. LOESScd is especially useful for estimating calibration curves when validating prognostic models.

papers.title: Unified conformalized multiple testing with full data efficiency
papers.authors: Yuyang Huo, Xiaoyang Wu, Changliang Zou, Haojie Ren
papers.abstract: Conformalized multiple testing offers a model-free way to control predictive uncertainty in decision-making. Existing methods typically use only part of the available data to build score functions tailored to specific settings. We propose a unified framework that puts data utilization at the centre: it uses all available data—null, alternative, and unlabelled—to construct scores and calibrate p-values through a full permutation strategy. This unified use of all available data significantly improves power by enhancing nonconformity score quality and maximizing calibration set size while rigorously controlling the false discovery rate. Crucially, our framework provides a systematic design principle for conformal testing and enables automatic selection of the best conformal procedure among candidates without extra data splitting. Extensive numerical experiments demonstrate that our enhanced methods deliver superior efficiency and adaptability across diverse scenarios.

papers.title: Saddlepoint approximations for plug-in resampling
papers.authors: Z Niu, Z Huang, J Ray Choudhury, E Katsevich
papers.abstract: Resampling-based procedures can improve on normal approximations in sparse, large-scale testing problems, but their computational cost can be prohibitive. We recognize that several existing procedures belong to a faster plug-in resampling subclass, fixing fitted nuisance parameters during resampling. When the resampled statistic is a sum of conditionally independent terms, the saddlepoint approximation for the resampling p -value offers further acceleration, replacing resampling with an analytical tail approximation. However, standard Edgeworth-based approximation-error bounds impose regularity conditions that are hard to verify for plug-in resampling laws. We use an alternative approach to establish a finite-sample relative-error bound for the Lugannani–Rice approximation under more tractable conditions, which we apply in two contexts. In statistical genetics, we identify response resampling procedures as the targets of existing saddlepoint approximations and establish guarantees in a representative setting. In conditional independence testing, we introduce a saddlepoint approximation for the distilled conditional randomization test, which has been applied successfully in biology. Our rates quantify the effects of sparsity and signal strength, with matching lower bounds in special cases. We additionally establish asymptotic Type-I error control of the corresponding plug-in resampling procedures under growing sparsity. In simulations and single-cell CRISPR data analysis, our new test closely approximates distilled conditional randomization test p -values and preserves its statistical performance while accelerating computation by up to 250-fold.

papers.title: Optimal Two-Phase Sampling Designs for Generalized Raking Estimators With Multiple Parameters of Interest
papers.authors: Jasper B Yang, Bryan E Shepherd, Thomas Lumley, Pamela A Shaw
papers.abstract: Large observational datasets, including those derived from electronic health records, are a valuable resource for medical research but are often affected by missingness, measurement error, and misclassification. Two-phase sampling with generalized raking (GR) estimation is an efficient and robust approach to statistical inference in such settings. In this approach, variables that are unavailable or measured with error in a large Phase 1 cohort are obtained with higher-quality measurements in a Phase 2 subsample. Previous research has studied optimal Phase 2 sampling designs for inverse-probability-weighted (IPW) estimators in nonadaptive, multiparameter settings, and for GR estimators in single-parameter settings. In this work, we extend these results by deriving optimal adaptive, multiwave sampling designs for IPW and GR estimators when multiple parameters are of interest. We propose several practical allocation strategies, examine the design choices that arise when implementing them, and evaluate their performance through extensive simulations and an example using data from people living with HIV attending the Vanderbilt Comprehensive Care Clinic (VCCC). Our results show that independently optimizing allocation for each parameter improves efficiency over traditional case-control sampling. We also derive an integer-valued, A-optimal allocation method that typically outperforms independent optimization. Notably, we find that optimal designs for GR can differ substantially from those for IPW, and that this distinction can meaningfully affect estimator efficiency in the multiple-parameter setting. These findings offer practical guidance for future two-phase studies involving incomplete or error-prone data.

papers.title: Multiscale Spatio-Temporal Data Monitoring Using Forward Elimination and Scale Information Criterion
papers.authors: Kai Yang, Peihua Qiu
papers.abstract: Spatio-temporal process monitoring has broad applications in disease surveillance, environment monitoring, epidemiology, and many other areas. Most existing spatio-temporal process monitoring methods are developed for analyzing observed data at a single geospatial scale (e.g., state, county, or census tract), and usually impose some parametric assumptions on spatio-temporal data structure. For instance, observed data are often assumed to follow a parametric distribution (e.g., normal or Poisson) and the mean and covariance of a related spatio-temporal model are assumed to have parametric forms, which are rarely valid and/or difficult to justify in many applications. In practice, spatio-temporal data (e.g., incidence rates of infectious diseases) are usually managed at multiple geospatial scales and have complicated structure. In this paper, we develop a new method for multiscale spatio-temporal data monitoring. At each observation time, the new method first detects anomalous regions at each spatial scale. To reduce computing time, a forward elimination procedure is suggested for this purpose. Then, an optimal spatial scale at the current observation time is determined using the detected anomalous regions and a proposed scale information criterion. Finally, a charting statistic is constructed based on the detected anomalous regions at the optimal scale. This method is fully nonparametric in the sense that no parametric assumptions are imposed on the structure of observed spatio-temporal data. It is also scalable and computationally efficient, making it a reliable and effective tool for online multiscale spatio-temporal data monitoring problems. *(abstract via OpenAlex)*

papers.title: Design and Analysis Strategies for Pooling in High Throughput Screening: Application to the Search for a New Anti-Microbial
papers.authors: Byran J Smucker, Benjamin Brennan, Emily Rego, Meng Wu, Zhihong Lin, Brian M M Ahmer, Blake R Peterson
papers.abstract: A major public health issue is the growing resistance of bacteria to antibiotics. An important part of the needed response is the discovery and development of new antimicrobial strategies. Require the screening of potential new drugs, typically accomplished using high-throughput screening (HTS). Traditionally, HTS is performed by examining one compound per well, but a more efficient strategy pools multiple compounds per well. In this work, we study several recently proposed pooling construction methods, as well as a variety of pooled high-throughput screening analysis methods, in order to provide guidance to practitioners on which methods to use. This is done in the context of an application of the methods to the search for new drugs to combat bacterial infection. We discuss both an extensive pilot study as well as a small screening campaign, and highlight both the successes and challenges of the pooling approach.

papers.title: Clinically Interpretable Time-To-Event Testing in Randomized Clinical Trials: Milestone Survival Combined With Restricted Mean Survival Time
papers.authors: Siwen He, Ludovic Trinquart
papers.abstract: The log-rank test and hazard ratio (HR) are widely used to compare survival curves in event-driven randomized clinical trials (RCTs). The optimality of the log-rank test and interpretation of the HR rely on the proportional hazards (PH) assumption, which is frequently violated in oncology due to delayed, waning, or crossing hazards. Although combination procedures built from weighted log-rank tests improve robustness to non-PH, hazard-based summaries remain difficult to interpret clinically. We propose combination tests that integrate two clinically interpretable estimands: the between-group difference in milestone survival probability S ( τ ) and in restricted mean survival time (RMST) μ ( 0 , τ ) . Using Monte Carlo simulations under a milestone-based design (uniform follow-up to τ ) and supplementary event-driven designs, we compared the proposed combinations with the log-rank and MaxCombo tests across diverse survival patterns, sample sizes, and censoring rates. We evaluated Type I error and power. The milestone combination procedures showed rejection probabilities close to the nominal level under the estimand-null configurations examined and showed competitive to superior power in non-PH settings, including transient effects and crossing hazards. Applications to three oncology RCTs illustrate that, when HRs hover near unity while absolute estimands differ, the milestone combinations can detect benefits at clinically meaningful horizons. These findings support aligning design, estimands, and analysis around a prespecified milestone. Careful selection of τ is essential to balance information and interpretability. Milestone-based combination tests provide a viable, patient-centered alternative or complement to HR-centric methods, particularly when non-PH is anticipated.

papers.title: A Max 0-1 Weighted Log-Rank Test for Time-to-Event Data With Random Delayed Treatment Effect
papers.authors: Jiarui Liu, Chenghao Chu, Bingming Yi, Ming-Hui Chen
papers.abstract: In a cancer clinical trial with an immunotherapy, the treatment often becomes effective after a certain delay time. It is well known that traditional log-rank test no longer provides optimal power in this case. There has been a great interest to search for a more powerful test to detect a truly effective immunotherapy treatment. In this paper, we propose a new testing method based on the maximum value of a set of 0-1 weighted log-rank test statistics and establish useful theoretical results of the relevant test statistics. Extensive simulation studies are conducted to examine the empirical performance of the proposed method. An analysis of the real data from a non-small-cell lung cancer clinical trial is also carried out to further demonstrate the usefulness of the proposed test method. Trial Registration: ClinicalTrials.gov ID: NCT01903993, NCT02008227.
